cf.title: Optimize mergejoinscansel() by avoiding redundant computations

input.subject: Optimize mergejoinscansel() by avoiding redundant computations

verdict_reasoning: The proposal is clear and claims unchanged estimates, but demand-1 survives at level 1b. Every number comes from synthetic queries on copies of pg_class on one laptop, and the saving is about 0.05 ms per qualifying statement. The author asks in the thread whether the gain is worth it, and nobody has answered. The verdict rests on missing evidence in a thread with one participant, so confidence is low.

brief.title: Skip redundant estimation work in mergejoinscansel() for equivalent inputs
brief.problem: When both inputs of a merge clause are the same column or expression of the same relation, mergejoinscansel() computes the same ranges and estimates twice and then discards them for the default result. This costs planning time in self-joins and joins against pulled-up subqueries and views, since scalarineqsel() may probe an index for the actual min/max.
brief.proposed_design: A new mergejoin_vardata_equivalent() runs after examine_variable() and decides whether the two inputs must give identical estimates. If so, and the operator is not cross-type, mergejoinscansel() skips get_variable_range() and scalarineqsel() and returns the default, adding stanullfrac for nulls-first when a range exists. Assert-enabled builds repeat the full computation via mergejoinscansel_internal() and check that both results match.
user_visible_surface: get_variable_range() in selfuncs.c now accepts NULL for min and max, and then only reports whether a range is available.
author_claims: Estimates and plans are unchanged; 29 merge join test cases give identical EXPLAIN output, costs included.
In steady state, mergejoinscansel() is about 96% faster and planning time about 20% lower when the shortcut applies.
When the shortcut does not apply, the extra check is lost in noise; one cold-connection case was about 0.3 ms slower, attributed to cache warming moving.
Regression, isolation and most TAP tests pass, and the assert cross-check caught an injected bug.
brief.thread_state: Only the author has posted, across five messages and four patch versions; no other reviewer has replied. The author asked for feedback on the correctness of the equivalence conditions and whether the gain is worth it.
unclear: The material does not show how often self-joins on the same column occur in real workloads compared with the synthetic tests.
The author does not say whether extensions outside core call get_variable_range() with the old contract.
The material does not show whether the pointer equality test on statistics tuples holds when a stats hook supplies data.
Benchmarks ran on one laptop under WSL1; there are no numbers from other hardware or with many merge clauses.

objections.title: No evidence that same-column merge self-joins cost real users planning time
objections.failure_scenario: A committer takes on new equivalence logic in selfuncs.c to save about 0.05 ms per qualifying statement. Afterwards, no user can be shown whose workload plans many same-column merge self-joins where this time matters.
objections.argument: Every number comes from synthetic queries on copies of pg_class, run on one laptop under WSL1 (messages #1, #3, #5). Message #1 calls the pattern "common" but cites no field report, -general or -bugs thread, or production profile. The author asks in messages #1 and #5 whether the gain justifies the work, and no one else has replied. The 20% saving applies only to statements that are already cheap to plan, about 0.245 ms.
objections.author_must_show: Which real workloads, such as ORM-generated views or reporting queries, spend measurable planning time on same-column merge clauses, and how large is that share in a profile?

critic.reasoning: The material shows only synthetic queries on copies of pg_class on one laptop, with a saving of about 0.05 ms per statement. The brief lists real-workload frequency as unknown, and the author asks whether the gain is worth it.

other_surviving.title: Equivalence rules become a second copy of selectivity internals
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later patch teaches scalarineqsel() or get_actual_variable_range() to use per-side information, such as varnullingrels, extended statistics or a hook result. mergejoin_vardata_equivalent() still returns true, so release builds return the default range while the full path would not. Nobody notices unless a regression test hits that exact case with assertions enabled.
other_surviving.argument: Message #5 says the rules "could drift if those functions change" and relies on an assert-only cross-check. That check runs only for queries the regression suite plans with the shortcut taken, which is 29 hand-picked cases plus whatever regress happens to cover. Each future change to selfuncs.c estimation then requires the author of that change to know that this predicate exists and to update it, with no failure in production builds. The verify_compact_attribute() precedent guards a cache of catalog data, which is a narrower invariant than the behaviour of an estimator.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which regression tests make the assert cross-check fail if scalarineqsel() starts to depend on a field that mergejoin_vardata_equivalent() does not compare?

critic.reasoning: Message #5 itself says the rules could drift, and release builds have no check. The assert cross-check runs on every assert-enabled regression run, but only catches drift for query shapes the tests plan with the shortcut taken.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Planner time saved is small and limited to one query shape
refuted.failure_scenario: The project accepts a fast path that saves about 0.05 ms per statement for merge joins between the same column of the same relation. Other estimator functions then gain similar special cases on the same argument, each with its own equivalence predicate and assert cross-check. selfuncs.c becomes harder to change safely for small total gain.
refuted.argument: Message #5 reports planning time going from about 0.245 ms to 0.195 ms, but only for self-joins on the same column, and only when a merge join path is costed. The numbers come from one laptop under WSL1. The thread shows no field report or workload where this planning time matters, and no reviewer has replied. The same reasoning would justify equivalent shortcuts in eqjoinsel() or other paired-estimate code, so a committer would likely ask for evidence of demand first.
refuted.author_must_show: Which real workload plans many same-column self-joins via merge join, and how much of its total planning time does mergejoinscansel() account for?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1 on the missing demand evidence. The remaining part, that eqjoinsel() or other estimators would gain similar shortcuts, is speculation; the proposal does not suggest that.

refuted.title: Small gain for one query shape adds a lasting coupling for selfuncs.c
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch changes what scalarineqsel() or get_variable_range() looks at, for example a stats hook or a new statistics kind. The shortcut then returns different estimates for self-joins. This shows up only if an assert-enabled test happens to run that path.
refuted.argument: Message #5 says the equivalence rules "could drift" and adds an assert-only cross-check to catch it. Everyone who later changes selectivity code pays for that coupling, while only users with same-column merge clauses gain. The rubric's accumulation test applies here: ten such shortcuts in selfuncs.c, each saving a few tens of microseconds for one query shape, would make that file harder to change safely. The material does not weigh this cost against the size of the user group.
refuted.author_must_show: How large must the planning-time saving be on a realistic workload to justify a rule set that every future change to scalarineqsel() must keep in sync?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1: the failure scenario is the same drift between the equivalence rules and scalarineqsel(). The question of gain against group size is covered by demand-1.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: get_variable_range() in selfuncs.c now accepts NULL for min and max; this widens the contract that extensions can call.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a shortcut in mergejoinscansel(); the author claims estimates and plans stay the same.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: mergejoin_vardata_equivalent() must stay in sync with what get_variable_range() and scalarineqsel() read; only an assert-only cross-check guards it.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Every mergejoinscansel() call runs the new equivalence check, including calls where the shortcut does not apply.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: No evidence that same-column merge self-joins cost real users planning time

questions: Which real workloads spend measurable planning time on same-column merge clauses, and what share of planning time does mergejoinscansel() take in a profile of them?
Does the pointer equality test on statistics tuples still hold when a stats hook supplies the data for one or both sides?
Which regression tests make the assert cross-check fail if scalarineqsel() starts to depend on a field that mergejoin_vardata_equivalent() does not compare?
What does the extra check cost on other hardware, and with many merge clauses where the shortcut does not apply?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the selectivity estimation code in selfuncs.c and how examine_variable() fills VariableStatData would have to own it. Only the author has posted.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the claim that the shortcut never changes an estimate, and for keeping the equivalence rules in sync with get_variable_range() and scalarineqsel() for as long as the shortcut exists. Release builds have no check.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted four patch versions in five messages and wrote in message #1 that they will continue the work if the direction is found promising.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: A profile or field report from a real workload, for example queries over views or ORM-generated self-joins, where same-column merge clauses take a measurable share of planning time. Numbers from more than one machine would also help.

priority.reason: The patch is small and touches one file, but a reviewer must check the equivalence conditions against the estimator code. The material shows a saving of about 0.05 ms per qualifying statement and no workload that needs it.

provisional_note: Level 2 was not evaluated; one design objection about drift between the equivalence rules and the estimator functions survived and waits there. Whether the rules keep estimates unchanged with stats hooks or pulled-up subqueries cannot be judged without the code.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
Reverted commit(s): Further reduce overhead for passing plpgsql variables to the executor.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This patch does three interrelated things:

* Create a new expression execution step type EEOP_PARAM_CALLBACK
and add the infrastructure needed for add-on modules to generate that.
As discussed, the best control mechanism for that seems to be to add
another hook function to ParamListInfo, which will be called by
ExecInitExpr if it's supplied and a PARAM_EXTERN Param is found.
For stand-alone expressions, we add a new entry point to allow the
ParamListInfo to be specified directly, since it can't be retrieved
from the parent plan node's EState.

* Redesign the API for the ParamListInfo paramFetch hook so that the
ParamExternData array can be entirely virtual.  This also lets us get rid
of ParamListInfo.paramMask, instead leaving it to the paramFetch hook to
decide which param IDs should be accessible or not.  plpgsql_param_fetch
was already doing the identical masking check, so having callers do it too
seemed redundant.  While I was at it, I added a "speculative" flag to
paramFetch that the planner can specify as TRUE to avoid unwanted failures.
This solves an ancient problem for plpgsql that it couldn't provide values
of non-DTYPE_VAR variables to the planner for fear of triggering premature
"record not assigned yet" or "field not found" errors during planning.

* Rework plpgsql to get rid of the need for "unshared" parameter lists,
by dint of turning the single ParamListInfo per estate into a nearly
read-only data structure that doesn't instantiate any per-variable data.
Instead, the paramFetch hook controls access to per-variable data and can
make the right decisions on the fly, replacing the cases that we used to
need multiple ParamListInfos for.  This might perhaps have been a
performance loss on its own, but by using a paramCompile hook we can
bypass plpgsql_param_fetch entirely during normal query execution.
(It's now only called when, eg, we copy the ParamListInfo into a cursor
portal.  copyParamList() or SerializeParamList() effectively instantiate
the virtual parameter array as a simple physical array without a
paramFetch hook, which is what we want in those cases.)  This allows
reverting most of commit 6c82d8d1f, though I kept the cosmetic
code-consolidation aspects of that (eg the assign_simple_var function).

Performance testing shows this to be at worst a break-even change,
and it can provide wins ranging up to 20% in test cases involving
accesses to fields of "record" variables.  The fact that values of
such variables can now be exposed to the planner might produce wins
in some situations, too, but I've not pursued that angle.

In passing, remove the "parent" pointer from the arguments to
ExecInitExprRec and related functions, instead storing that pointer in a
transient field in ExprState.  The ParamListInfo pointer for a stand-alone
expression is handled the same way; we'd otherwise have had to add
yet another recursively-passed-down argument in expression compilation.

precedents_retrieved.title: Document efficient self-joins / UPDATE LIMIT techniques.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds documentation examples that show how to update or delete rows in batches, using a CTE with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and `LIMIT` and a self-join on the system column `ctid`. It offers this as a documented workaround while `UPDATE` and `DELETE` have no `LIMIT` clause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback because Laurenz Albe's review comments were not yet resolved. His comments covered redundant examples, the stated rationale and wording. Corey Huinker then sent a revised patch, and Laurenz Albe judged it close to ready for committer. The author had reopened the entry in the commitfest that was already closed, so Laurenz Albe closed it again and moved the patch to a new entry in the open commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I closed that again and added a new entry in the open commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: plpgsql - possibility to get element or array type for referenced variable type
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets PL/pgSQL `%TYPE` refer to variables of composite type, including polymorphic parameters. It also adds syntax to derive the array type or the element type of a referenced variable, first as `%ARRAYTYPE`/`%ELEMENTTYPE` and later as `%TYPE[]` and `ELEMENT OF ...%TYPE`.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane proposed rejecting this PL/pgSQL-only implementation. He wanted these type operators added to the core grammar's Typename production, so PL/pgSQL would pick them up automatically. Joe Conway and Jim Nasby agreed. The author then found that a reduced patch with only the composite `%TYPE` fix gave too little benefit, and asked for it to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I played with the reduced patch, and the benefit without all other things
is negligible. It should be rejected.

precedents_retrieved.title: SLOPE - Planner optimizations on monotonic expressions.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set lets the planner use an index on x to satisfy ordering on f(x) when f is monotonic, which removes sorts and allows GroupAggregate and index-based min/max for queries such as `group by date_trunc('month', ts)`. It adds slope prosupport functions to many built-in casts, operators and math and date functions, plus an `enable_slope` setting.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Review by Zsolt Parragi found correctness bugs in interval arithmetic, NULL ordering, infinities and NaN, domains, and timestamptz to timestamp casts across a DST change, and the author fixed or removed each one. The last message, on the day the entry was withdrawn, is the author posting a further fix with no stated reason for withdrawal.

precedents_retrieved.title: minimizing pg_stat_statements.track='none' performance overhead
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pgss_post_parse_analyze in pg_stat_statements return early when pgss_enabled() is false, so that pg_stat_statements.track = 'none' skips query jumbling and query text storage. The goal is to cut the extension's overhead without a restart to remove it from shared_preload_libraries.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last message reports that the same patch has two commitfest entries (2080 and 2092) and asks which one to keep, so this entry may have been withdrawn as a duplicate. Robert Haas asked what happens if pgss_enabled() changes between processing stages, but no message treats this as blocking.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove redundant NULL check in clause_selectivity_ext()
precedents_retrieved.summary: Remove the NULL clause check in clause_selectivity_ext(), which carries a "can this still happen?" comment, because no core caller seems to pass a NULL clause. The author listed each core call site to support this.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane wanted the check kept because it is cheap and extensions call clauselist_selectivity and related functions and may rely on it not crashing on a NULL. He also said the list_length check proves nothing about NULL list elements, and that removing such checks one at a time without agreed invariants is not wise. David Rowley agreed, saying no speedup could be measured and no benchmark was given, and suggested marking the entry rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Certainly, such an assumption could be argued to be a bug they
should fix; but I'm disinclined to make them jump through that
hoop for a vanishingly small performance improvement.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reduce timing overhead of EXPLAIN ANALYZE using rdtsc
precedents_retrieved.authors: Andres Freund (andresfreund), Lukas Fittl (lfittl), David Geier (geidav)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make instr_time count CPU reference cycles read with rdtsc, which does not wait for prior instructions, and convert cycles to time only on output, to cut the timing overhead of EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The patch uses rdtsc only on Linux/x86 when the kernel clocksource is tsc, takes the TSC frequency from CPUID, and falls back to clock_gettime() otherwise.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stopped after the v8 patch of February 2023, and nobody continued the work for about a year. vignesh C closed the entry as Returned with feedback because neither the author nor anyone else took it forward. Earlier, Andres Freund doubted the patch was ready on reliability and code complexity, citing the Linux-only restriction, but the entry closed from inactivity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since the author or no one else showed interest in taking it forward
and the patch had no activity for more than 1 year, I have changed the
status to RWF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Skip a redundant singleton GROUP BY node
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch series lets the planner skip a plain GROUP BY step, adding projection paths in place of aggregate paths, when a unique index on a single base or partitioned table proves each input row is its own group. Patch 1 moves the unique-index matching logic out of remove_useless_groupby_columns() into a shared helper.
precedents_retrieved.objection: David Rowley noted that this was the author's third new thread on the topic in about three weeks, and that the idea is proposed regularly on the list. He also pointed to earlier discussions and to a patch for the same thing already in the commitfest, and advised against pursuing this one. The author agreed to review those proposals and the existing patch; the entry was then withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
For this one, I wouldn't bother as the idea gets proposed regularly on
this mailing list.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. The only row, [P11], is about removing a NULL check from clause_selectivity_ext(), a different idea. Its recorded reasons, an unmeasured gain and a narrower contract for extensions, do not apply here: this proposal shows measurements, and get_variable_range() now accepts more inputs (NULL min/max), so existing callers keep working. Message #1 cites CommitFest 7302 only as the author's other work, not as an earlier attempt at this idea.

The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object, dump content or psql change, and claims unchanged estimates and plans. Its one interface change, get_variable_range() accepting NULL min and max, only widens the contract, so existing extension callers keep working. Whether the equivalence rules really keep estimates unchanged, for example with stats hooks or pulled-up subqueries, is a correctness question for the design angle. It cannot be checked without the code.

The patch touches only planner estimation in selfuncs.c and adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, wire protocol or replication state. The get_variable_range() change only widens what callers may pass, so existing calls keep working and extensions are not broken.

The patch has no new privilege or exposure surface: no new object, setting, function or view, and the shortcut returns the default estimate without reading statistics. The proposal requires equal acl_ok and keeps the nulls-first stanullfrac rule, which leaves leakproofness and RLS behaviour as in master. Whether the NULL-min/max path of get_variable_range() keeps the operator security check depends on the code and cannot be judged here.
The get_variable_range() change accepts NULL in addition to the old contract, so existing extension callers are not affected; no objection raised there.

No existing feature or extension does this job. The per-clause cache in cached_scansel() avoids repeat calls for one merge clause, but it does not skip the duplicate work inside one mergejoinscansel() call, and this planner-internal shortcut cannot be built as an extension.
Two objections are raised. Both are of the not-now kind: the material shows no demand beyond synthetic benchmarks, and no other reviewer has replied yet.
